Youtuber here- every week I produce a game news show- this week was no exception. Generally, what I look for in a Youtuber is somebody who's making things that I'm interested in hearing about. For instance, I love watching stuff like Every Frame a Painting in which a director's style is broken down and explained clearly and concisely. That's what's keeps me coming back- I love what Tony does on his channel, and it's clear that Tony loves what he's doing.

The same thing applies to gaming Youtubers. When they put the time and effort into making interesting and informative content, I'm willing to give them my views- it's that simple. Folks like Totalbiscuit, for instance, really care about giving good coverage of a game- even if it's not a game the person's fond of. For instance, he played this game called Lethis once, and he wasn't really fond of it- his audience told him that the things he criticized weren't really flaws but were actually integral to the genre of game- so he gave the game another shot. It still wasn't the game for him, but he went to the trouble of making sure it was covered accurately. That's the sort of Youtuber I want to be.

Speaking as a Youtuber, here's some stuff I've learned about having a channel:

  • Regularity is critical. When I first started making my show, I was all over the place with when it came out- I eventually settled on a runtime and airdate, and I stick to it.

  • Listening to your audience is important. When my show first started, it was rife with problems. Listening to the people who were watching it helped me to improve. My show's still not technically perfect- I process my audio as best I can, but I think I just need to invest in a new microphone now- nonetheless, everybody's feedback made my show a lot better.

  • Watching my own content. It's not enough to just make something, run through it quickly and assume it's good enough. That's like writing a book, assuming it's good enough and trying to get it published- you have to really be familiar with your own work! You'll get better at noticing flaws, realizing where your pacing sucks, etc., and then understand how to fix whatever it is that needs fixing.

Do you ever feel self conscious when you view your previous work?

An audience can give you great critique, although it can be quite annoying when it seems like every improvement you make leads to another critique. I guess that's a unique struggle as a youtuber in that, you have to juggle what people say and understand what needs adjusting and what needs to remain.

I don't really feel self conscious, though I do sometimes feel a little frustrated looking back at recent work and realizing dangit, I can't believe I didn't know technique X or what have you- but generally? I feel great when I look back, recognize what needed improvement and realize that I made the changes.

And yeah, it's good to listen to your audience but just be careful not to overdo it, you know? If you try to please everybody you'll make nobody happy- especially not yourself.

True true. I've met a lot of people (artists, musicians, among other youtubers) who are self conscious of their old work. There are times when I struggle with it but push myself to be more accepting and loving of my content.
